AVALON CITY COUNCIL MEETING
  TUESDAY, JUNE 20, 2023 5:00 PM  —

  410 AVALON CANYON ROAD
  THIS VIRTUAL MEETING IS HELD PURSUANT TO AB 361
  AGENDA

  In compliance with the Americans with Disability Act! if you need special assistance to participate in this
  meeting! please contact the City Clerk’s Office (310) 510-0220. Notification 48 hours prior to the meeting wiN
  enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to ensure accessibility to this meeting. (28 CFR 35. 102-
  35.104 ADA Title II). All public records relating to an agenda item on this agenda are available for the public
  inspection at the time the records are distributed to all! or a majority of all, members of the City Council. Such
  records shall be available at City Hall located at 410 Avalon Canyon Rd.

Due to social distancing recommendations from the Center for Disease Control and State of
California Division of Occupational Safety and Health (Cal/OSHA) and the County of Los
Angeles, and pursuant to findings made under AS 361, the CITY OF AVALONS CITY COUNCIL
SHALL GENERALLY BE AVAILABLE TO THE PUBLIC REMOTELY. The general public may
attend the meeting in the Council Chambers however must adhere to social distancing
requirements. The public is encouraged to watch and participate from the safety of their homes
while practicing social distancing.

Council Chambers are open to a maximum 30 members of the general public. Once the Council
Chambers reach maximum occupancy, the general public may participate in Oral
Communication and address the City Council on an agenda item in person by waiting in the City
Hall Court Yard and entering the Chambers one at a time at the appropriate time. No one will be
admiffed into the Council Chambers who is ill or exhibiting symptoms of COVID-1 9. Additionally,
the general public may participate in Oral Communication and address the City Council on an
agenda items by providing comments via Zoom or by sending comments to
askcityofava Ion .com.

  For the public’s convenience, but not participation, the meeting can be viewed:
  On local cable: Catalina Broadband Solutions channel 3
  Streaming Online: www.cityofavalon.com/meetings
  *streaming on Facebook Live: www.facebook.com/CityOfAvalonOfficial
  Streaming on YouTube: https:Jlwww.youtube.com/CityofAvalonCA

  Passcode: 756380

When you would like to comment during the meeting enter *9 on the phone’s key pad to
activate the “raise hand” button at the time the Agenda Item is being presented for City Council
consideration.

ORAL COMMUNICATION
Members of the public may address the City Council at this time. No action will be taken on non-
agenda items at this meeting. Speakers should limit comments to two (2) minutes each.

PRESENTATIONS:

  1. A representative from Avalon Environmental Services, Inc. will provide an overview of
  implementation of recycling standards mandated by SB 1383.

CONSENT CALENDAR

1.  Minutes
  Although the live recording is the official record of public meetings, actions are prepared
  for the Council’s approval.
  Recommended Action
  Approve minutes from the June 6, 2023 regular City Council Meeting.

2.  Warrants
  Expenditures Submitted for Approval
  o Warrants in the amount of $870,336.11.
  o One payroll in the amount of $224,056.48.
  o Three electronic fund transfers totaling $106,516.36.
  Recommended Action
  Approve the total expenditures for May 29, 2023 through June 9, 2023 totaling
  $1,200,908.95.

3.  Findings to Continue to Hold Remote Teleconference/virtual City Council Meetings
  Pursuant to Assembly Bill 361
  As the State of Emergency has ended, the City Council can continue to hold virtual
  meetings without providing notice of the City Council’s teleconference location if the City
  Council makes the following two findings: 1. State or local officials have imposed or
  recommended measures to promote social distancing in connection with COVID-19; and
  2. The City Council reconsiders the circumstances of the state of the emergency and
  danger presented by COVID-1 9; Having made the findings, the City Council can continue
  every 30 days to authorize meetings under AR 361 to protect the health or safety of
  attendees.
 CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
JUNE 20, 2023
PAGE 3

  Recommended Action
  Reconsider the circumstances of COVID-19 state of emergency proclaimed by the
  Governor and COVID-19’s continued impact and determine that state or local officials
  have imposed or recommended measures to promote social distancing in connection with
  COVID-19, and as such, that continuing to utilize the protections of Assembly Bill 361 will
  protect the health and safely of attendees.

4.  Gann Appropriations Limit for Fiscal Year 2023-2024
  The City is required to review and adopt a resolution approving the annual appropriations
  limit to ensure the City is not over taxing its payers. The proposed budget for FY23-24
  has been reviewed and the tax proceeds of the General Fund are within the limit.
  Recommended Action
  (1) Adopt the resolution committing $1,000,000 from the City’s General Fund unassigned
  fund balance to the City’s Capital Reserve Fund (Fund 106), and (2) adopt the resolution
  approving the Annual Gann Appropriations Limit calculation for Fiscal Year (FY) 2023-
  2024.

5.  Law Enforcement Services Agreement with Los Angeles County
  Annually, the City Council submits an authorization form establishing the annual fee for
  Los Angeles County to provide law enforcement services to the City of Avalon. The
  estimated cost of services for FY 23-24 is $1,822,417.52.
  Recommended Action
  Adopt a resolution notifying the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors of the City’s
  desire to receive specified law enforcement services from the Los Angeles County
  Sheriff’s office, authorizing the expenditure of COPS Grant Funds and authorize the City
  Manager to execute the Service Level Authorization Form (SH-AD 575) for FY 23-24.

6.  Resolution Approving Application for TDA Article S Funds
  Adopt the Resolution approving the annual application for Transit Development Act (TDA)
  funds for Fiscal Year 2023.
  Recommended Action
  Adopt the Resolution approving the annual application for Transit Development Act (TDA)
  funds for Fiscal Year 2023.

7.  City Manager Employment Agreement Merit Increase
  —

  On May 16. 2023, the City Council completed the annual performance evaluation for the
  City Manager, in accordance with the terms of the employment agreement. City Council
  directed staff to prepare an amendment to the compensation section of the Employment
  Agreement to provide a 5% merit increase to the City Manager’s base salary.
  Recommended Action
  Amend the compensation terms of the Employment Agreement for City Manager Services
  with David Maistros dated December 10, 2021, providing a 5% merit increase to the City
  Manager’s base pay retroactively effective beginning on the first anniversary of
  employment (February 1, 2023).
 CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
JUNE 20, 2023
PAGE 4

PUBLIC HEARING

8.  Public Hearing to Receive Comment on the City’s FY 23-24 Community Development
  Block Giant (CDBG) Funds
  The City participates in the Los Angeles County Community Development’s Community
  Development Block Grant Program. Per the terms of the program, the City provided a 30-
  day public notice for members of the public to submit public comment in advance of a
  public hearing to review the City’s proposed revisions to the CDBG Consolidated Plan.
  Recommended Action
  1. Open the duly noticed Public Hearing and receive comment. 2. Close the Public
  Hearing. 3. Approve the City’s estimated FY 23-24 Community Development Block Grant
  (CDBG) Funds for Phase II of the ADA Curb and Ramp Project. 4. Adopt a resolution
  authorizing the allocation of CDBG Funds for Fiscal Year 23-24.

GENERAL BUSINESS

9.  Consideration of Transportation Permit Haunted Catalina Ghost Tour, LLC
  —

  On June 1, 2023, Jessica Hickman, dba Haunted Catalina Ghost Tour, [[C, submitted a
  Transportation Permit application to the City of Avalon to provide transportation services
  to individuals interested in a guided golf cart ghost tour.
  Recommended Action
  Discuss and provide direction. If consensus for approval is reached, make the affirmative
  finding that the criteria set forth in Avalon Municipal Code Section 5-14.04 has been met
  and award a Transportation Permit to Haunted Catalina Ghost Tours, LLC pending
  confirmation of permit conditions being met.

10.  Amendment to Professional Services Agreement with Catalina Falconry, LLC
  On March 3, 2023, Catalina Falconry, [[C requested a contract increase in order to
  increase the number of shoulder season flights in order to assist in maintaining bay water
  quality. The increase number of shoulder season flights will focus on the gull brooding
  and hatching window that occurs from January through March.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize the City Manager to amend the Professional Services Agreement for bird
  abatement services with Catalina Falconry, LLC for an amount not to exceed $79,200
  annually for the remainder of the existing contract term expiring May 25, 2024.

11.  Geo-[ogic Associates Contract Award
  the City received a report last month from Montrose Water and Sustainability Services,
  Inc. estimating the Pebbly Beach Landfill will be at capacity by July 31, 2027. Council
  received a presentation from Geo-Logic Associates on a proposal to extend the life of the
  landfill by completing a vertical expansion project. The expansion would add
  approximately 20-25 years to the life of the landfill.
 CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
JUNE 20, 2023
PAGE 5

  Recommended Action
  Authorize the City Manager to execute a contract with Geo-Logic Associates for a not-to-
  exceed sum of $520000.

12.  Proposed Fiscal Year 2023-24 Budget
  Based on input received during tour preceding City Council budget study sessions, Staff
  is presenting the proposed Fiscal Year 2023-24 Operating and Capital Budget for City
  Council to review and consider for adoption. The proposed budget also includes updates
  to the City’s Budget and Fiscal Policies, which includes the Statement of Investment
  Policy, for review and adoption, as well.
  Recommended Action
  Continue discussing the proposed Fiscal Year 2023-24 Budget. If consensus, adopt a
  resolution establishing the City budget for Fiscal Year 2023-24.

ADJOURN

on Friday, June 16, 2023 on the City’s website www.cityofavalon.com/agendacenter, and at City
Hall, 410 Avalon Canyon Road.

Devin Elise Hart, Management Analyst

   AVALON CITY COUNCIL MEETING
  TUESDAY, JUNE 6, 2023 4:30 P.M. —

  THIS VIRTUAL MEETING IS HELD PURSUANT TO AB 361
  MINUTES

Due to social distancing recommendations from the Center for Disease Control and
State of California Division of Occupational Safety and Health (Cal/OSI—IA) and the
County of Los Angeles, and pursuant to findings made under AB 361, the CITY OF
AVALON’S CITY COUNCIL SHALL GENERALLY BE AVAILABLE TO THE PUBLIC
REMOTELY. The general public may attend the meeting in the Council Chambers
however must adhere to social distancing requirements. The public is encouraged to
watch and participate from the safety of their homes while practicing social distancing.

Council Chambers are open to a maximum 30 members of the general public. Once the
Council Chambers reach maximum occupancy, the general public may participate in
Oral Communication and address the City Council on an agenda item in person by
waiting in the City Hall Court Yard and entering the Chambers one at a time at the
appropriate time. No one will be admitted into the Council Chambers who is ill or
exhibiting symptoms of COVID-19. Additionally, the general public may participate in
Oral Communication and address the City Council on an agenda items by providing
comments via Zoom or by sending comments to askcityofavalon.com.

CALL TO ORDER-4:30 p.m.

ROLL CALL Present via Teleconference and In-Person: Mayor Anni Marshall,
Councilmembers Lisa Lavelle, Michael Ponce, Mary Schickling and Yesenia De La
Rosa. Also present: City Manager David Maistros, City Attorney Scott Campbell and
Deputy City Clerk Gabrielle Morones.

  2. Finance Director Matthew Baker provided an overview of the proposed budget

CONSENT CALENDAR-There were 5 Items on the Consent Calendar. Motion to

1.  Minutes
  Approved minutes from the May 16, 2023 regular City Council Meeting.

2.  Warrants
  Approved warrants in the amount of $1,787,000.12, including $496,448.09 CIMC

  electronic fund transfers totaling $62,087.84 for a total disbursement of

3.  Findings to Continue to Hold Remote Teleconference/Virtual City Council
  Meetings Pursuant to Assembly Bill 361
  Reconsidered the circumstances of COVID-19 state of emergency proclaimed by
  the Governor and COVID-19’s continued impact and determined that state or

  distancing in connection with COVID-19. and as such, that continuing to utilize
  the protections of Assembly Bill 361 will protect the health and safety of
  attendees.

4.  Cooperation Agreement for Continued Participation in the Los Angeles Urban
  County Community Development Block Grant Program
  Authorized the City Manager to execute the cooperation agreement with the Los
  Angeles County Development Authority for a three-year term beginning July 1,
  2023— June 30, 2027 and adopted Resolution No. 23-10 of the City Council of
  the City of Avalon Approving Participation in The Los Angeles Urban County
  Program.

5.  Resolution Adopting List of Projects for Annual SB1 Allocation
  Adopted Resolution No. 23-11 of the City Council of the City of Avalon Adopting
  a List of Projects for Fiscal Year 2023-24 Funded by SB 1: The Road Repair And
  Accountability Act of 2017.

PUBLIC HEARING

6.  Fiscal Year 2023-2024 Miscellaneous Fee Schedule
  1. Heard a presentation regarding the Miscellaneous Fee Schedule. 2. Mayor
  Marshall opened the Public Hearing, no comments were heard. 3. Mayor
  Marshall closed the Public Hearing. 4. Adopted Resolution No. 23-12 of the City
  Council of the City of Avalon Setting Fees for Services, Facilities and Activities of
  the City of Avalon for Fiscal Year 2023-24.
  Motion to approve made by Michael Ponce, seconded by Lisa Lavelle. (All Ayes)

7.  Public Hearing Regarding Resolutions Adopting the Reports Proposing to Have
  Sewer, Saltwater, Solid Waste Collection Service, and Grease Collection Service
  Charges Collected on the Property Tax Roll for Fiscal Year 2023-24 and
  Directing the City Clerk to File Said Report with the Los Angeles Auditor-
  Controller to Place Said Charges on the Tax Roll
  1. Mayor Marshall opened the public hearing on whether to collect the annual
  solid waste collection service charges, grease collection service charges, sewer
  charges, and saltwater charges (collectively, the “Charges”), on the property tax
  roll by the County of Los Angeles. No comments were heard and Mayor
  Marshall closed the Public Hearing. It was determined that there was not a
  majority of property owners who submitted formal written protest to the proposed
  Sewer1 Saltwater. Solid Waste, and Grease rate increases.

  2. Adopted four resolutions adopting reports of the annual sewer charges
  (Resolution No. 23-13), saltwater charges (Resolution No. 23-14), solid waste
  collection charges (Resolution No. 23-15), and grease collection charges
  (Resolution No. 23-16).

  Motion to approve made by Lisa Lavelle, seconded by Mary Schickling.
  (All Ayes)

8.  TDA Article 8 Hearing
  Mayor Marshall opened the Public Hearing, no comments were received from the
  public and Mayor Marshall closed the Public Hearing.

GENERAL BUSINESS- Item #9 was removed at the request of the applicant.

9.  Contract Assignment for Semi-Exclusive Shore Boat Franchise and Shore Boat
  Services Provider Agreement
  This item appears on the agenda at the request of representatives from Catalina
  Coastal Tours, LLC. The City Council considered a request from Catalina
  Coastal Tours, LLC to assign the remaining term of the semi-exclusive shore
  boat franchise agreement to Catalina Coastal Shoreboat Service, LLC. The City

  Consider a request to assign the remaining term of the semi-exclusive shore boat

SUBJECT:  Findings to Continue to Hold Remote Teleconference/Virtual City
  Council Meetings Pursuant to Assembly Bill 361

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Reconsider the circumstances of COVID-1 9 state of emergency
proclaimed by the Governor and COVID-19’s continued impact and determine that state or local
officials have imposed or recommended measures to promote social distancing in connection
with COVID-19, and as such, that continuing to utilize the protections of Assembly Bill 361 will
protect the health and safely of attendees.

REPORT SUMMARY: Traditionally, the Brown Act allows for teleconference or virtual meetings,
provided that the physical locations of the legislative body’s members joining by teleconference
are posted on the agenda, that those locations are open to the public and that a quorum of the
members is located within its jurisdiction. AB 361 provides an exception to these procedures in
order to allow for fully virtual meetings during proclaimed emergencies, including the COVID-19
pandemic.

Since March of 2020 and the issuance of Governor Newsom’s Executive Order N-29-20, which
suspended portions of the Brown Act relating to teleconferencing, the City Council has had virtual
meetings without having to post the location of the legislative body members attending virtually.
Most public agencies have been holding public meetings using virtual platforms since this time.
In June of 2021. Governor Newsom issued Executive Order N-08-21, which provided that the
exceptions contained in EO N-29-20 would sunset on September 30, 2021.

On September 10, 2021, the Legislature adopted AB 361, which allows public agencies to hold
fully virtual meetings under certain circumstances without the posting of the agenda from each
location a legislative body member is attending. Governor Newsom signed the bill into law on
September 16,2021. Because it contained an urgency provision, it took immediate effect.

Specific Findings Required underAB 361

As the State of Emergency has ended, the City Council can continue to hold virtual meetings
without providing notice of the City Council’s teleconference location if the City Council makes
the following two findings:

  1. State or local officials have imposed or recommended measures to promote social
  distancing in connection with COVID-19; and

  2. The City Council reconsiders the circumstances of the state of the emergency and danger
  presented by COVID-19;
65059.00000\3452048 I I
 Having made the findings, the City Council can continue every 30 days to authorize meetings
under AS 261 to protect the health or safety of attendees.

COVID-1 9 continues to present a threat to the health or safety of members of the public. Although
vaccines are now widely available, many people in the State and County are still not fully
vaccinated and remain susceptible to infection. The disease can still spread rapidly through
person-to-person contact and those in close proximity. According to the most recently published
data, 5.5% of those tested statewide for COVID-1 9 tested positive, an increase of 1.0% from the
prior week. Additionally, Cal/OHSA has implemented COVID-19 Prevention Non-Emergency
Regulations that will remain in effect until February 3, 2025. The City’s economy is dependent
upon visitors to the island, the presence of which, increases the likelihood of transmission of the
disease. Also, having members of the public attend council meetings at locations where council
members are in attendance due to their desire to avoid exposure to COVID-19 poses a risk to
the health or safety of attendees.

Re-Authorization is Required Within 30 Days

The City Council made the required findings at its June 6, 2023 City Council meeting. Consistent
with the provisions of AS 361, the new findings must be made every 30 days. Thus, if the City
Council desires to continue to meet remotely without having to post the location of each
teleconference location, the City Council reconsider the facts of the state of emergency and
continued impact of COVID-19, find that state or local officials have imposed or recommended
measures to promote social distancing in connection with COVID-19, and therefore, that remote
meetings under AS 361 should continue in order to protect the health or safety of attendees.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City Council will
have to follow the Brown Act provisions that existed prior to the COVID-1 9 pandemic.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: That the City Council make the findings under AS 361 at its July 18,
2023 City Council meeting.

SUBJECT:  Gann Appropriations Limit for Fiscal Year 2023-2024

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): (1)Adopt the resolution committing $1,000,000 from the City’s
General Fund unassigned fund balance to the City’s Capital Reserve Fund (Fund 106), and (2)
adopt the resolution approving the Annual Gann Appropriations Limit calculation for Fiscal Year
(FY) 2023-2024.

REPORT SUMMARY:
In November 1979, California voters approved Proposition 4 (the “Gann Initiative”) which is
included in Article XIIIB of the California Constitution. Proposition 4 limits the amount of tax
revenue that State and local government agencies can appropriate. In June 1990, California
voters approved changes to the base year calculation and provided cities with more flexibility in
the selection of certain inflation and population factors used to determine the appropriations limit.
The City’s annual appropriations limit is calculated based upon the level of appropriations in the
base year and subsequent changes in the local population and cost of living. During any fiscal
year, the City may not appropriate any proceeds of taxes received in excess of the appropriations
limit of the entity. If the City receives excess funds in any one year, it may carry those funds into
a subsequent year for use. Any excess funds after the second year must be returned to
taxpayers by reducing tax rates or fees.

The City is required by the California State Constitution to annually establish and adhere to a
limit on the amount of its appropriations as prescribed by the State. During FY 202 1-2022, the
City of Avalon adopted a resolution approving an appropriations of $9,059,210 subject to the
limit, which was $3,412,384 or 37.67% under the limit. The appropriations subject to the limit
were calculated based on revenue estimates included in the FY 2021-2022 Budget. The
budgeted revenues, developed during the spring of 2021, were estimated conservatively given
the City’s reserve levels and continued economic uncertainty arising from the pandemic;
however, visitor-driven tax revenues, particularly transient occupancy tax (TOT), significantly
exceeded pre-pandemic averages during FY 2021-2022, with TOT alone exceeding estimates
used in the appropriations limit calculation by $3.5 million. Based on tax revenues received in
FY 2021-2022, actual appropriations exceeded the limit by S895,489 during the fiscal year. The
City elected to carry those funds into the subsequent tax year.

During FY 2022-2023, the City approved an appropriations subject to the limit of $7,212,768,
which was $6,105! 198 or 45.84% under the limit. The appropriations subject to the limit included
allowable exclusions for qualified capital outlays, including the Five Corners Pedestrian
 Improvement Project, Pebbly Beach Road Revetment Project, and the Crescent Avenue Hillside
Rehabilitation Project. In FY 2022-2023, tax revenues will likely exceed estimates used to
determine the amount of appropriations subject to the limit and qualified capital outlays will not
reach the amounts excluded from the calculation due to changes in project timelines. However,
appropriations subject to the limit are still estimated to be under the limit by $922,171, which
covers the overage from the prior fiscal year.

In addition to qualified capital outlays, contributions to a capital reserve fund may be excluded
from the appropriations subject to limitation. Given that FY2022-2023 tax revenues include
estimates for the last quarter of the fiscal year, the margin for compliance between FY2021 -2022
and FY2022-2023, and the City’s intent to expend the qualified capital outlays in the upcoming
fiscal year, Staff recommends transferring $1,000,000 in unassigned General Fund balance to
its Capital Reserves Fund (Fund 106). This will ensure that the City remains in compliance with
its appropriation limit requirements in the event that actual revenues exceed current estimates
for FY2022-2023.

For the upcoming FY 2023-2024, the City expects to collect and has budgeted to appropriate
$11,564,988 subject to the limitation, which is $2,239,976 or 16.23% under the appropriation
limit. Staff utilized the percentage change in per capita income and annual percentage change
in County population to determine the appropriations limit. The appropriations subject to the limit
only excludes Measure H Tax collections used to fund the new hospital construction, with the
previously identified projects to be funded with the dedicated capital reserves. The attached
schedules provide detailed information on the City’s appropriation limit calculation for FY 2023-
2024.

As required in Article XIIIB, the City Council must authorize both inflation and population factors
for calculating the spending limitation amount. The available options are:

  1. Inflation Factors
  a. California per capita income
  b. Growth in the nonresidential assessed valuation due to new construction within the
  City.
  2. Population Factors:
  a. City population growth
  b. County population growth

Staff recommends the selected combination of factors that result in the City’s ability to retain the
greatest flexibility under the spending limitation. The two factors that accomplish this objective
for the FY23-24 limit are the California per capita income and the County population growth. By
selecting the recommended combination of factors, the City reserves the highest level of
management discretion for future appropriations.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Required Reporting

 CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City would be out
of compliance with State law by not approving the factors and adopting the Appropriations Limit
for FY23-24.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: File certified copy of adopted resolution.

SUBJECT:  Law Enforcement Services Agreement with Los Angeles County

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Adopt a resolution notifying the Los Angeles County Board of
Supervisors of the City’s desire to receive specified law enforcement services from the Los
Angeles County Sheriff’s (LASD) office, authorizing the expenditure of COPS Grant Funds and
authorize the City Manager to execute the Service Level Authorization Form (SH-AD 575) for
FY 23-24.

REPORT SUMMARY: The attached authorization form establishes the annual fee for Los
Angeles County to provide law enforcement services to the City for FY 23-24. The estimated
cost of services in FY 23-24 totals $1,822,417.52.

During the June 21, 2022 meeting of the City Council, the City Council authorized the City
Manager to execute the authorization form for FY 22-23 totaling $1,659,588.78. For FY 22-23,
the Los Angeles Sheriff Department (LASD) proposed increasing the number of paid deputies
from 5 to 5.5. This change accounted for approximately $135,918 of the overall increase to the
contract. The additional manpower allowed the local Station Commander to have greater
flexibility with schedule and more manpower to support the City’s needs. In FY 22-23 the
additional manpower was contracted as a specialized rate identified as a “Growth Deputy
Generalist.” In FY 23-24, the rate changes to a standard Catalina Deputy.

LASD works with 46 contract cities. Unlike other cites, the City of Avalon receives a special
“Catalina Deputy” rate for services. From FY 21-22 to FY 22-23 the ‘Catalina Deputy” rate
increased from $271,836 to $295,845. The “Catalina Deputy” rate is an approximate $28,371
savings per deputy over other cities.

Additionally, LASD does not charge the City a salary for its Station Commander, six additional
deputies, four 911 emergency dispatchers, a portion of a jailer salary, use of various public
safety equipment including all department vehicles and boats or any other supplemental
  —  —

services.

Per the terms of the contract, the City of Avalon has the option to request additional reserve
deputies to provide public safety services on an as needed basis. The City does not pay these
reserve deputies a salary, but the City does cover their travel, hotel accommodations and
reimbursements for meals. Historically, the City has hired reserve deputies on popular
weekends throughout the year as well as during cruise ship days. The fees for these reserve
deputies are not included in the regular contract.
 From FY 22-23 to FY 23-24 the total contract cost is projected to increase by approximately
$162853.74. There are two elements of the contract: cost of services and the liability trust
fund allocation. The cost of services increased slightly in converting the 0.5 Growth Deputy
Generalist to a Catalina Deputy. The liability trust fund is the Contract Cities self-insurance
and is allocated to members by multiplying the total cost of services provided by an approved
percentage. The liability trust fund cost allocation percentage increased by 1% from 11% in FY
22-23 to 12% in FY 23-24.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Contract amount of $1822417.52 is budgeted in the FY 23-24 Budget, in
the General Fund account 10240-5110.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City will not have
an executed contract with the Los Angeles Sheriffs Department.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Execute authorization form and send to Contract City Law
Enforcement Services.

ADVERTISING, NOTICE AND PUBLIC CONTACT: Pursuant to the Brown Act.

SUBJECT:  City Manager Employment Agreement  —  Merit Increase

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Amend the compensation terms of the Employment Agreement
for City Manager Services with David Maistros dated December 10, 2021, providing a 5% merit
increase to the City Manager’s base pay retroactively effective beginning on the first anniversary
of employment (February 1, 2023).

REPORT SUMMARY: On November 16, 2021, the City Council authorized the execution of the
Employment Agreement for City Manager Services with David M. Maistros.

Per the City of Avalon’s Personnel Rules and Regulations, Chapter 2, Section 11.1: “The City
Manager is directly responsible to the City Council for the successful administration of the City.
The salary range for the City Manager position shall be established by the Council. The Council
shall periodically review the salary of the City Manager. Changes to the salary of the City
Manager shall be at the discretion of the City Council.”

  Employer shall pay Employee a salaty of Two Hundred Ten Thousand Dollars ($210,000)
  per year in accordance with Employer’s regularly established policies for payroll
  distribution. Employee will receive cost of living increases as may be provided to other
  City employees during the term of the Agreement. Employee is also eligible for merit
  increases during the term of this Agreement at the discretion of and as may be negotiated
  by the City Council. In no event shall Employee’s salaty decrease during the terms of the
  Agreement unless specifically agreed to by Employee and the City

Manager, in accordance with the terms of the employment agreement. City Council directed staff
to prepare an amendment to the compensation section of the Employment Agreement to provide

budget of $218,284.

curb ramps at various locations throughout the City.

SUBJECT:  Consideration of Transportation Permit  —  Haunted Catalina Ghost
  Tour, [[C

RECOMMENDED ACTION: Discuss and provide direction. If consensus for approval is
reached, make the affirmative finding that the criteria set forth in Avalon Municipal Code
Section 5-14.04 has been met and award a Transportation Permit to Haunted Catalina Ghost
Tours, [[C pending confirmation of permit conditions being met.

REPORT SUMMARY: On June 1, 2023, Jessica Hickman, dba Haunted Catalina Ghost Tour,
LLC, submitted a Transportation Permit application to the City of Avalon to provide
transportation services to individuals interested in a guided golf cart ghost tour. The business
currently operates a guided walking tour. Per the applicant, a transportation permit will allow
the business to reach a larger audience by providing tour opportunities to individuals with
limited mobility.

From a predetermined pick up location, the tour will proceed through much of Avalon including
Wrigley Terrace Road to Pebbly Beach Road, Descanso Beach, the Botanical Gardens,
portions of Falls Canyon, as well as Metropole, Whittley and ManIla Avenues. Predetermined
pick up and drop off location will include hotels, vacation rentals, People’s Park, Descanso
Beach or near Metropole Marketplace.

The business proposes to utilize a 2004, gasoline powered, Yamaha Limo, 6 passenger golf
cart. The vehicle will be required to have a new commercial autoette as the business owner
plans to continue to utilize their residential autoette for non-business related activities.

Per the Avalon Municipal Code Section (AMC) 5-14.04, the City Council must make the
determination whether a transportation permit should be approved. Per the AMC:

Sec. 5-14.04 (b)  Permits: Applications: Requirements.*

  (b)  The Council may grant a permit upon the proposed terms or upon terms other
  than those proposed. The Council shall make the initial permit grant, and the Vehicle
  Clerk may thereafter renew a permit if he is able to make affirmative findings based on
  the criteria set forth below. If the Vehicle Clerk is unable to make the affirmative
  findings, he shall so advise the permit holder and set a hearing date before the Vehicle
  Hearing Officer, whose decision on the renewal shall be appealable to the City Council
  in accordance with the procedures set forth in Title 1, Chapter 4.:
   (1)  The applicant has presented facts demonstrating a necessity for the
  requested vehicle(s).

  (2)  The requested vehicle(s) is appropriate for the intended use and
  necessary, for the proper functioning of the applicant’s enterprise:

  (3)  The requested vehicle(s) will not have a deleterious impact on traffic
  congestion, traffic safety, noise or air pollution:

  (4)  In view of the size and nature of the streets of the City and the character of
  the City itself, the requested vehicle(s) will not have a deleterious impact on the public
  health, safety, and welfare:

  (5)  There is no more suitable alternative vehicle than the vehicle(s) requested
  by the applicant that can satisfy its requirements.

  (6) In the case of renewal only, the requested vehicle has been used and
  continues to be used in accordance with the terms and conditions of the permit.

If this transportation permit is approved by the City Council, the applicant must go before the
Vehicle Hearing Officer to receive approval of a commercial autoette in addition to meeting
other standard permit conditions. The applicant has stated she has secured off street parking
at the St. Catherine of Alexandria Catholic Church.

Other conditions that must be met before a permit may be issued include:
  • Provide written permission from the Catalina Island Company to operate on private
  roads, and
  • Provide proof of insurance meeting standards as described in the AMC.

Upon renewal each year the Vehicle Clerk will evaluate if the business model has adversely
added to the traffic, safety, and congestion in Avalon.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Potential for nominal additional revenue to the City through taxes.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: N/A

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Implement City Council direction.

SUBJECT:  Amendment to Professional Services Agreement with Catalina
  Falconry, LLC

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize the City Manager to amend the Professional
Services Agreement for bird abatement services with Catalina Falconry, LLC for an amount not
to exceed $79,200 annually for the remainder of the existing contract term expiring May 25,
2024.

REPORT SUMMARY: The City had contracted with On the Wing Falconry for many years as
part of its program to comply with Cease and Desist Order pertaining to the cleanliness of
Avalon Harbor waters. The bird abatement program has been part of the City’s success in
establishing and maintaining Harbor water quality and mitigating the City’s pest bird issues.

Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, and as a component of the City’s attempt to reduce
expenditures, the City terminated the agreement with On the Wing Falconry in July 2020. A
new agreement with On the Wing Falconry was drafted in mid July 2020 that reduced the
scope of services, schedule and total compensation associated with the program. When that
agreement expired in October 2020 the City did not renew it in order to further reduce
expenditures.

After COVID-19 restrictions were relaxed, the need for pest bird abatement became apparent
again.

David Long of Catalina Falconry, [[C approached City Staff with an interest in reestablishing
the bird abatement program in January 2021.

On April 6, 2021 the City Council authorized the City Manager to enter into a three year
agreement for bird abatement services with Catalina Falconry, LLC for an amount to exceed
$60,000 for an initial period of three years expiring on May 25, 2024 with two optional one
  —  —

year renewal terms.

In light of the COVID-19 pandemic, the contract agreement outlined a reduced rate to provide
bird abatement services:

  $250 per half day of service through FY2O-21.
   •  $275 per half day of service for the first six months of FY21 -22.
  •  $300 per half day of service for the second six months of FY21 -22.
  •  After year one, an annual CPI increase (if applicable).

A half day of service is defined as a four hour period, with three hours of actual flight time.

On March 3, 2023, Mr. Long requested a contract increase in order to increase the number of
shoulder season half day flights as such flights are needed to maintain water quality. The exact
days of the week and time of day will be determined by Mr. Long, though scheduled to be a
minimum number of times per month, so that it is most effective in mitigating the pest bird
issues. The increase number of shoulder season flights will focus on the gull brooding and
hatching window that occurs from January through March. This service has been critical to
maintaining the high grades the City has received for harbor water quality and helps the City
remain in compliance with clear water regulatory requirements.

Mr. Long provides a monthly flight log for City Staff to ensure adherence to the contracted
terms.

For Fiscal Year 2023-24, a combination of sewer funds within account 10725-5017
(approximately $53,000) and General Funds within account 10350-5017 (approximately
$27,000) will support this program.

GOAL: Pest bird abatement.

FISCAL IMPACTS: For Fiscal Year 2023-24, a combination of sewer funds within account
10725-5017 (approximately $53,000) and General Funds within account 10350-5017
(approximately $27,000) will support this program.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: Visitor dissatisfaction
due to bird nuisances and potential increase in bay water bacteria levels.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Draft and execute amendment.

REPORT SUMMARY: The City of Avalon received a report last month fromMontrose Water
and Sustainability Services, Inc. estimating the Pebbly Beach Landfill will be at capacity by July
31, 2027.

In 2022, Avalon Environmental Services, Inc. (CR&R) completed a contract with Geo-Logic
Associates to complete Task 1 of the attached proposal, which included developing a project
description, conducting analysis on alternative projects, and completing early consultation with
City stakeholders and CR&R. In January 2023, City Council received a presentation from Geo
Logic Associates and CR&R on a proposed scope to extend the life of the landfill by completing
a vertical expansion project. The expansion would add approximately 20-25 years to the life of
the landfill.

If approved by City Council, Geo-Logic Associates will work with City staff, and CR&R in
preparing the Conditional Use Permit (CUP) application, Coastal Development Permit (CDP)
application, conducting special technical studies, preparing CEQA documentation, and working
with Los Angeles County Regional Planning. Depending on initial determinations, Geo-Logic
Associates will complete a Mitigated Negative Declaration (MND) or Environmental Impact
Report (EIR). Below are the total proposals costs for each potential alternative depending on
initial findings.

Due to the extremely limited time frame of the life of the landfill, the different agencies that will
require approvals, and the logistics of the project in general, it is recommended the City move
forward with the firm that already has experience and knowledge of the proposed project.
Although City staff and CR&R will work on a major campaign with residents, businesses, and

estimates, as project completion estimates are extremely close to at-capacity estimates.
 The City of Avalon procurement ordinance allows the City to move forward with dispensing
competitive procedures where services may be obtained more economically or efficiently. Due
to the limited time frame of the project, it is recommended to award a contract to Geo-Logic

analysis and developing scope for the expansion of the landfill, as well as the existing working
relationship between CR&R and the City. The firm will have the ability to start the technical

Reference, Avalon Municipal Code §3-4.111 (c) Economic Efficiency. If a competitive market
does not exist, or the City will not gain a competitive advantage by using the formal contract bid
or other competitive procedure, or where the public project, goods or services may be obtained
more economically or efficiently without the procedure, the City may dispense with formal bidding

  Existing Site Conditions at Pebbly Beach Landfill
  The PBL is located in the unincorporated area of Los Angeles County, on the southeast edge of
  Santa Catalina Island (Catalina), south of the City of Avalon. The landfill is owned by the City of
  Avalon (COA) and CR&R operates the landfill, Materials Recovery Facility (MRF), and compost
  operation under contract with CDA. Because the site is located on an island offshore from the
  continental United States, the United States Geological Survey (USGS) does not provide a
  Section, Township, Range, Baseline, or Meridian location reference. The location of the disposal
  site is therefore given as 332 19’ 18” N Latitude and 118 19’ 4” W Longitude. Access to the site
  is from the north, via Pebbly Beach Road to Dump Road, which traverses the east side of the
  disposal site. The airport on the Island is located approximately eight miles to the north of the
  landfill and the flight pattern is not near the landfill. There is also a heliport terminal located
  approximately one-half mile north of the landfill.

  The PBL site was originally a rock quarry that was used to provide riprap for coastal marine
  projects in the southern California area and elsewhere. The excavation into the existing steep
  natural terrain was conducted as a part of mining activities that were underway at the site
  before 1926. The site was graded level prior to the beginning of the landfill operations,
  sometime in the 1940’s or 1950’s.

  The site operated as an open burn dump until 1986 when a pit burner incinerator system was
  installed. The ash from the incinerator was deposited into the current landfill area along with
  sewage sludge from the sewage treatment plant located a few hundred feet to the north of the
  incinerator. Since approximately 2000, PBL has processed incoming solid waste to remove
  recyclables in the MRF building that was commissioned in 2000. The recyclable materials are
  baled and barged to the mainland. The organic materials are shredded and composted, and the
  remaining materials are baled and then landfilled.

  The PBL site is approximately 7.7 acres and is relatively isolated and visually secluded from
  adjacent land uses by the surrounding mountainous terrain. The nearest structures are the
  contractor’s sheds and storage buildings on adjacent leased land and the City of Avalon
  wastewater treatment plant, located approximately 800 feet northwest of the disposal site. No
  permitted residential developments (or other sensitive receptors) are adjacent to or within
  1,000 feet of the PBL.

  Los Angeles County (County) designated zoning at and within 1,000 feet of the disposal site is
  Utility and Industrial District. The Assessors’ Parcel Number (APN) for the site is 7480-45-900.
  The 1983 Santa Catalina Island Local Coastal Plan identifies existing and planned land use within
  this area and refers to the general area as the Pebbly Beach service area. The Pebbly Beach
  service area is comprised of industrial services for the City of Avalon, operated by the Santa
  Catalina Island Company or their contractors. The Pebbly Beach service area includes a sewage
  treatment plant, a desalinization plant, an electric power and gas distribution plant, an oil bulk
  storage facility, a commercial amphibian airplane and heliport terminal, boat and mooring

  designated wastes, other hazardous wastes or other wastes requiring special handling are
  accepted at the site. Construction/demolition debris and salvageable materials are placed in
  roll-off bins, and recyclable materials recovered in the MRF are baled for recycling and are not
  landfilled. Green waste and source separated food waste are processed on site for windrow
  composting.

  The average daily traffic volume is approximately twenty-five to thirty-five vehicle trips per day.
  Commercially owned vehicles comprise a majority of the vehicle traffic at the site, with an
  approximate distribution of 95 percent commercial refuse haulers and 5 percent public haulers.
  According to waste inventory records, incoming refuse loads include the following vehicle types:
  CR&R trucks, City vehicles, Contract Haulers, private vehicles, and construction roll offs.

  Proposed Project
  GLA proposes to extend the life of the site primarily through the construction of an up to 18-
  foot-high retaining wall placed at the toe of slope (eastern most boundary of the 5.6-acre limit
  of waste). Waste will be filled against the retaining wall and project back to the top deck at an
  average grade of 2:1 H:V, allowing sufficient space to construct a final cover system that will tie
  into a concrete v-ditch installed along the top of the wall to intercept and divert surface water
  to the original discharge locations. The permitted height of the PBL would increase from its
  current height by approximately 50 feet.

  No changes to waste volume or composition are anticipated. No increase in permitted daily
  tonnage is anticipated. The MRF, landfilling, and composting facility operations are not
  anticipated to change.

  Task 4.3 Biological Resources Assessment Survey and Report
 The County considers the biological resources in the Santa Catalina Island Coastal Zone to be of
 significance. Biological resource management and regulation in the Santa Catalina Island
 Coastal Zone is implemented through the Santa Catalina Island Local Coastal Program; PBL is
 located within the Southeast Santa Catalina Island Critical Coastal Area, which is managed as an
 Area of Special Biological Significance.

  A comprehensive Biological Resources Assessment (BRA) report will be prepared to address the
  baseline biological conditions that could be affected by the proposed project and will be of
  sufficient detail to satisfy CEQA analysis and regulatory permitting. The focus of the BRA will be
  to inventory and assess the possible sensitivity of biological resources affected by the project
  and identify measures to avoid, minimize and/or mitigate potential effects to state and
  federally listed species and/or other sensitive biological resources. This task includes a review
  of existing literature sources, a reconnaissance-level field survey, and preparation of the BRA
  which will incorporate the findings of the field investigation, assess potential impacts to
  sensitive biological resources, and develop recommendations to avoid, minimize, and/or
  mitigate potential impacts.

  Background Review and Reconnaissance Survey
  The GLA Team will review background information and project design plans (in CAD and/or GIS
  formats) in preparation of the reconnaissance-level field survey. Following the background
  review, our team will conduct a reconnaissance field survey to map vegetation communities
  and wildlife habitats and assess the site for the capacity to support special status species.

  Please note that the analysis of potential impacts to special status wildlife species will be based
  on a suitability analysis (i.e., habitat assessment) under this task and does not include definitive
  surveys for the presence or absence of special status species that may be present. Potential
  wetland features as defined under the California Coastal Act (CCA) will be surveyed. In contrast
  to wetland waters of the U.S. potential coastal wetland features are defined by the presence of
  one of the three USACE wetland indictors in accordance with California Code of Regulations
  Title 14. Definitive surveys for special status plant and wildlife species often require specific
  survey protocols involving extensive field survey time to be conducted only at certain times of
  the year. Similarly, this scope of work does not include mapping individual trees or completion
  of an arborist report. Upon completion of the field survey, The GLA Team will identify additional

  quartz diorite plutonic rock. In addition, the geologist will map the slope descending from
  Dump Road to the shoreline to evaluate the thickness of fill and alluvium, and the relationship
  of these materials to the underlying bedrock. Geologic contacts and attitudes will be mapped
  in the field using a Brunton compass, and a Trimble Geo7X GPS receiver will be used to record
  the locations of geologic features to the nearest foot. Data will be transferred to a topographic
  map of the site to develop figures for inclusion in permitting and CEQA documents.

  Drilling, Logging, and Sampling
  A small, truck-mounted hollow-stem auger drill rig will be transported to Catalina Island to
  facilitate drilling of three to four shallow boreholes along the alignment of the proposed
  retaining wall. Each borehole will be advanced to establish the depth to bedrock. Relatively
  undisturbed soil samples will be collected at five-foot intervals using a California-modified split-
  spoon sampler fitted with a series of brass rings to facilitate logging of the subsurface materials
  and evaluation of geotechnical characteristics. Representative samples will be retained for
  testing of shear strength. Samples will be tested by the GLA Team’s geotechnical laboratory in
  Anaheim, California for shear strength by ASTM 3080.

  Optional Task ReMI Geophysical Survey: If drilling cannot be performed due to access
  —

  restrictions or other conditions, The GLA Team will conduct a geophysical survey to establish
  the depth to bedrock along the alignment of the proposed retaining wall. The geophysical
  survey will be conducted using the refraction microtremor (ReMi) method, which utilizes
  ambient seismic noise to evaluate shear wave velocities in subsurface materials. Two arrays
  will be deployed to capture the shear wave data along the entire length of the proposed
  retaining wall. Data will be collected by driving a small vehicle along the arrays to generate the
  seismic energy that will be collected by the geophones and seismograph. The process data will
  be used to illustrate the soil/fill and bedrock profile along the proposed retaining wall
  alignment.

Honorable Mayor, Members of the City Council, and Community Members of the City of
Avalon, California:

I am pleased to submit for your consideration the Fiscal Year (FY) 2023-2024 Operating and
Capital Improvement Budget for the City ofAvalon (City). This document implements the direction
provided by the City Council and serves as a financial plan for the continued improvement of the
quality of life for Avalon residents, businesses and stakeholders.

Over the past fiscal year, the City of Avalon has successfully weathered a number of challenges,
with the focus on drought-related conservation efforts at the beginning of the year shifting to
remediation efforts from significant rainthll and storm damage by the end of the year. Despite the
unseasonable weather, the City of Avalon will meet or exceed its budgeted revenue estimates, as a
result of a strong summer season and conservative revenue estimates used in the development of
the current budget. This year highlighted the importance of this conservative approach, with
weather impacting visitor-driven tax revenues and fees.

The City completed a number of major capital improvement projects during the year, including the
construction of a new pump out float and the rehabilitation of the Casino Way Arch. The City also
completed the first phase of structural improvements to the Pleasure Pier (Green Pier), with plans
to complete the rehabilitation of the pier in phases over the next several fiscal years. In addition,
the City diligently pursued additional finding opportunities for several of its larger capital projects,
with over $10 million combined in new grant funds awarded for the Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal,
Five Corner Pedestrian Improvements, and Pebbly Beach Road Revetinent and Rehabilitation
projects. In the coming year, we will be allocating significant resources towards the construction of
these projects, which will provide improved pedestrian access and climate resiliency to critical
infrastructure.

The proposed FY 2023-2024 budget was developed using a conservative approach to revenue
allocation while meeting the community’s needs and addressing the priorities identified by City
Council. I am pleased to present you with the budget for Fiscal Year 2023-2024 that builds upon
the accomplishments of the prior fiscal year.

Budget Overview

Budget Process
Each year, the Avalon City Council adopts. by formal resolution, an annual budget. This docinnent
serves as a financial plan, identifying the projected allocation and application of resources over the
budget cycle. The published Operating and Capital Budget is designed to present summary
information about the City’s financial plans for the year in a user-friendly format. The budget is
organized by ilind and department. Expenditures are displayed and subtotaled by the following
types: Salaries & Benefits: Maintenance & Operations; Contract Services; and Capital Outlays.

Line-item budget development is accomplished through the Citys online budget system, which
allows each department to build its operating budget using computerized worksheets. The
individual departments are directly responsible for developing the Maintenance & Operations and
Contract Services expenditure budgets. The Salary & Benefit information is calculated and entered
by the Finance Department based on salary schedules and applicable memorandums of
understanding. New budget requests (e.g. new personnel services, equipment) are identified by
the Finance Director and presented separately for the City Manager’s review’ and approval before
becoming part of the proposed operating budget. The Finance Director also provides the City
Manager with revenue projections. These revenue esthmtes are reviewed with the department
budget requests to determine available thnding levels for the fiscal year. The City Manager and
Finance Director then hold meetings with the departments to review the operating budgets and
additional budget requests. Once the budget data has been reviewed and any changes have been
made by the Finance Department, a proposed budget document is prepared. Afier review and
approval by the City Manager, the proposed budget document is presented to City Council, with
at least one study session and public presentation, prior to adoption. During the fiscal year, the
budget can be amended as necessary by City Council to meet the City’s needs. The City’s budget
and fiscal policies outline internal controls for transfers within budgeted accounts.

Basis of Accounting
The Citys accounting system is maintained on a find basis, in accordance with governmental
accounting standards. Each of the City’s fluids is considered a separate accounting entity with a
selfbalancing set ofaccounts that records assets, liabilities, fund equity, reveniLes arid expenditures.
Funds are established and segregated for the purpose of recording specific programs or attaining
certain objectives in accordance with special regulations restrictions, or limitations.

Funds are classified into one of three categories: governmental (general find, special revenues),
proprietary (enterprise and internal service), and fiduciary (trust or agency). Governmental funds
account for activities generally associated with local governnEnt operations. Proprietary funds are
financed and operated in a manner similar to private business enterprises, where the intent is to
recover the costs ofproviding goods and services from users through charges for services. Fiduciary
finds are utilized in situations where the government is acting in a fiduciary capacity as a trustee.

The City budget is maintained using the modified accrual basis of accounting, which recognizes
revenues when they become measurable and available. Expenditures are recognized when the ifind
liability is incurred. For budget presentation purposes, the City records capital outlays as an expense
to assist with budgetary controL At year-end, the arniunts are converted to capital assets, as
appropriate, for presentation in audited financial statements. The City’s governmental finds are
also reported on a modified accrual basis of accounting in the City’s Annual Comprehensive
Financial Report (ACFR) find statements; however, the Enterprise and ffiternal Service Funds are
reported on a Ill accrual basis in the ACFR.

The following Classification of Funds describes, in detail, the various types of finds and their
purpose as established by the City of Avalon

GOVERNMENTAL FUND TYPES
General Fund is used to account for resources traditionally associated with general government
which are not required to be accounted for in a separate fund including: sales tax, property tax,
transient occupancy tax, licenses and permits, fines and forfeitures. This fund is used to finance
most of the basic municipal fhnctions, including public safety, community services, planning and
public works. Other non-major funds are aggregated with General Fund activity for budget
purposes.

Special Revenue Funds
The Street Adininistration Fund is used to account for the City’s share of State and County gaso line
tax collection in accordance with the provisions of the State of Califbrnia Streets and Highway
Code. Revenues are disbursed by the State based on population and must be used towards the
maintenance and repair of City streets.

The Traffic Safety Fund is used to account for fines collected and are used to find eligible traffic
safety and code enforcement expenditures. Expenditures in excess of fines collected are covered
through budgeted transfers from the General Fund.

The Community Development Block Grant (CDBG,) Fund is used to account for the receipts and
expenditures of CDBG fhnds received from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban
Development.

The Local Transportation Fund is used to account for the proceeds from Proposition A and C and
Measures R and M, additional sales tax generated by the approval of Los Angeles County voters
administered by the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transit Authority (MTA) for transportation-
related projects. These finds are used to support the cross-channel commuter subsidy program and
local public transportation, including fixed-route and dial-a-ride services.

Enterprise Funds
The Harbor Fund is used to account for all harbor operations, including the the! dock.

The Saltwater Fund was established to receive charges for the operation of the City’s sa!twater

The Solid Waste Fund was established to account for solid waste collection and disposal costs.

The Avalon Transit Fund was established to account for the portion of the City’s fixed route, dial-
a-ride, cross-channel commuter subsidy program, and other transportation operations not covered
by the Local Transportation Fund.

Internal Service Funds
The General Administration Fund is used to account for general administration costs, including the
City Manager’s office, finance, information technology, legal, provided to other finds and
departments on a cost reimbursement basis.

The Insurance Fund is used to account for the City’s genera! liability program.

The Vehicle Maintenance Fund is used to account for the operation, maintenance, and replacement
ofCity vehicles. Revenues are generated from each departments share of operating costs.

 Budget and Fiscal Policies
CITY OF AVALON

Presented for Adoption: June 20, 2023

  154
 The following policies outline the City of Avalon’s (City) guidelines for budgetary decision-making and
sets standards for sound budgetary practices and fiscal performance.
An adopted set of budget policies that are consistently followed will assist the City in achieving its current
and future goals in a fiscally responsible and sustainable manner. These policies establish guidelines for
developing and monitoring the City’s annual operating and capital budgets as recommended by the
Government Finance Officers Association (GFOA) and the National Advisory Council on State and Local
Budgeting (NACSLB). This document shall be reviewed on an annual basis to reflect the highest
standards of fiscal management and the City’s budgetary goals.
The City’s budget and fiscal policies have been organized under the followmg coiwonents:

  A.  Accounting and Annual Reporting
  B.  Budget Process
  C.  Structurally Balanced Budget
  D.  Revenues
  E.  Expenditures
  F.  General Fund Reserves
  G.  Enterprise Fund Working Capital Targets
  H.  Investment Policy
  I.  Investment Policy for Solid Waste Postclosure and Corrective Action Trust Fund

  155
 A. ACCOUNTING AND ANNUAL REPORTING POLICIES

  Purpose: The purpose of this policy is to ensure the proper recording of financial transactions and
  identif’ the parties responsible for financial reporting.

  Background:
  The City’s Comprehensive Annual Financial Report (CAFR) presents the government and its
  component units (entities for which the government is considered to be financially accountable)
  financial and operating activities. The City’s blended component units, although legally separate
  entities, are, in substance, part of the City’s operations and financial data from these units are
  combined with data of the City. The City’s financial statements and accounting records are niainta med
  in accordance with the recommendations of the Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB).

  The government-wide financial statements report information on all of the non-fiduciary activities of
  the primary government and its component units. For the most part, the effect of inter-find activity
  has been removed from these statements. Governmental activities, normally supported by taxes and
  inter-governmental revenues, are reported separately from business-type activities that rely, to a
  significant extent, on fees and charges for support.

  Separate financial statements are provided for governmental kinds, proprietary kinds, and fiduciary
  kinds, even though the latter are excluded from the government-wide financial statements. Major
  individual governmental kinds are reported as separate columns in the find financial statements. The
  government-wide financial statements are reported using the economic resources measurement focus
  and the accrual basis of accounting, as are the proprietary find and fiduciary find financial statements.
  Revenues are recorded when earned and expenses are recorded when a liability is incurred, regardless
  of the timing of related cash flows. Property taxes are recognized as revenues in the year for which
  they are levied. Grants and similar items are recognized as revenue as soon as all eligibility
  requirements imposed by the providers have been met. As a general rule, the effect of inter- Rind
  activity has been eliminated from the government-wide financial statements. Direct expenses have
  not been eliminated from the Ilinctional categories; however, indirect expenses and internal payments
  have been eliminated.

  Aimunts reported as program revenues include: 1) charges to customers or applicants for goods,
  services, or privileges provided; 2) operating grants and contributions; and 3) capital grants and
  contnbutions, including special assessments. Internally dedicated resources are reported as general
  revenues rather than program revenues. Lilcewise, general revenues include aU taxes.

  Governmental kind financial statements are reported using the current financial resources
  measurement focus and the modified accrual basis of accounting. Revenues are recognized as soon
  as they are both measurable and available. Revenues are considered available when they are collected
  within the current period or soon enough thereafter to pay liabilities of the current period. For this
  purpose, the City considers revenues available if they are collected within 60 days of the end of the
  current fiscal period. Fxpenditures generally are recorded when a liability is incurred, as under accrual
  accounting. However, debt service expenditures, as well as expenditures related to conwensated
  absences are recorded only when payment is due.

  156
 Taxes, licenses and interest associated with the current fiscal period are all considered to be
susceptible to accrual and are therefore recognized as revenues of the current fiscal period. Only the
portion of special assessments receivable due within the current fiscal period is considered to be
susceptible to accrual as revenue of the current period. All other revenue items are considered
measurable and available only when the City receives cash.

The City reports the following governmental hind types:

  •  General Fund has been classified as a major flind and is used to account for resources
  traditionally associated with governments which are not required legally or by sound financial
  management to be accounted for in another hind.
  •  Special Revenue Funds account for proceeds of specific revenue sources that are legally
  restricied or otherwise designated for specific purposes.
  •  Nonmajor Funds is the aggregate of all the other governmcnt funds.

The City teports the following proprietary funds:
  •  1-larbor Fund has hccn classified as an enterprise fund and is used to account for all harbor
  operations
  •  Sewer Fund has been classificd as an enterprise fOnd and is used to account for the fees and
  services fOr the operation and maintenance of sewer system.
  •  Saltwater Fund has been classified as an enterprise fund and is used to account for the
  operation of the City’s saltwater pumping plants and systems.
  •  Solid Waste Fund has been classified as an enterprise fOnd and is used to account for the solid
  waste collection and disposal costs.
  •  General Administration, Insurance, and Vehicle Maintenance have been classified as internal
  service funds and are used to account for operations that provide services to other departments
  of the C’ity on a cost reimbursement basis.
Additionally. the City reports its Success Agency activity in a Private-Purpose Trust Fund.

Policy:
Each year an audit will he conducted by an indcpendent Certified Public Accountant Firm (CPA
Firm). The selection of the independent CPA Firm shall be in conformance with the City’s
professional services bidding procedures. Generally, the City shall request bids for audit services no
less frequently than every five years. The CPA Finn shall provide the City Council with an Audit
Communication Lctter addressing significant findings of the auditors in conjunction with their
opinion on the City’s Comprehensive Annual FinanciaL Report. These reports shall be submitted to
the City Council within 60 days of receipt of the report.
During the annual budget process, the City will make available a preliminary year end, unaudited,
General Fund hind balance. It should be recognized, however, that the balance provided is subject to
both unforeseen financial transactions ofa material nature and subject to findings of the independent
audit. An audit verified year-end balance should be available by the end of December. The City will
use generally accepted accounting principles in preparing its annual financial statements, and will
strive to meet the requirements of the GFOA’s Award for Excellence in Financial Reporting program.

 B. BUTGET PROCESS

  Purpose:
  The purpose of this policy is to establish guidelines for the preparation, adoption, and presentation
  of the City’s annual budget.

  Background:
  The City ofAvalon operates on a fiscal year basis, starting July 1 and ending June 30. The budget is
  prepared by the Finance Department with the support of each operating department under the direct
  supervision of the City Manager. The Finance Department is responsible for coordinating all revenues
  estimates contained in the budget. Estimates are reached by analyzing historical revenue history,
  national and local economic ti-ends and indices, and development patterns in the local economy. The
  Finance Department also coordinates the development of the expenditure budgets with the support of
  each operating department and the City Manager.

  The budget is structured to separate operating and capital activity at the fund and department level.
  The operating budget is a guide for the receipt and disbursement of hinds used to provide daily,
  routine public services to the community. The operating budget is structured to include historical
  budget and actual revenues and expenditures. along with the current revenue estimates and proposed
  expenditures required in order to implement and maintain services to the community. The Capital
  Improvement Prota-am (OF) budget details the acquisitioa construction, or rehabilitation of major
  capital thcilities and infrastructure over a ten year period.

  Policy:
  The proposed budget ts to be presented to the City Council and community in pubhc workshop
  meetings in May or June for review, public input, and deliberation. After providing opportunities for
  public review and discussion at City Council workshops and City Council meetings, the budget is
  adopted by the City Council prior to June 30 at either a regular or special City Council Meeting. The
  City Council may amend or supplement the budget at any time after its adoption by majority vote of
  the Council Members.

  The budget document should incorporate the Ihllowing guidelines to facilitate broader consumption
  and greater comprehension. The document should be organized in a manner that reduces redundancy
  and allows for a logical flow- of information. The budget document should include an introduction
  and overview, financial summaries, operating and capital detail, departmental intbrmation, and a
  glossary. The document should avoid excessive detail, which can distract from the primary points
  presented, and should present the information in a consistent manner across departments and budget
  years.

 C. STRUCTURALLY BALANCED BUI)GET

  Purpose:
  The purpose of this policy is to establish guidelines for the City’s operating hinds aimed at achieving
  and maintaining a structural]y balanced budget. State law requires that the City adopts a balanced
  budget. However, a budget that is balanced by the state’s definition may not necessarily be structurally
  balanced or sustainable if recurring expenditures are covered by reserves or non-recurring or highly
  volatile revenues. This policy supports the on-going financial stability of the City by advancing a
  more sustainable definition of a balanced budget a structurally balanced budget.
  —

  Background:
  This section defines key terms related to a structurally balanced budget:

  Recurring Revenues are the portion of the City’s revenues that can reasonably be predicted to
  continue year-to-year. with some degree ofpredictability. Property taxes are an example ofa recurring
  revenue. Non-recurring Revenue are revenues that are one-time in nature and cannot he reasonably
  expected to cotitinue year-to-year.

  Some revenue sources may have both recurring and non-recurring components. These sources require
  the City to exercise judgment in determining how much of the source is truly recurring. For example.
  the City regularly receives tran.sfer fees for the sale of nnorings in the harbor; however, the amount
  received varies year-to-year based on the value of moorings and number of sales. In this case, it may
  be prudent to regard tumsually high transfer revenues as non-recurring revenue under the assumption
  that such revenues are unlikely to continue, making it imprudent to u.se them for recurrrng
  expenditures.

  Recurring expendh!ure.c appear in the budget each year. Salaries, benefits, rent, utilities, maintenance
  costs and certain contracted services are coinnxm examples of recurring expenditures. In general.
  recurring expenditures should he those that the City expects to fond every year in order to maintain
  current service levels. Non-recurring expendhnres comprise special projects. .sich as capital
  improvements, asset acquisitions, and other costs incurred infrequently by the City. In general. the
  City has a greater degree of flexibility to defer non-recurring expenditures than recurring ones.

  Reserves are the portion of lund balance set aside as a hedge against risk. The City has defined a
  minimum amount of hinds it will hold in reserve. This serves as a ‘bottoni line measure” to help
  deternine the extent to which the City’s structural balance policy is being met  —  if reserves are
  maintained  at their desired levels, it is an indication that the City is maintaining a structurally  balanced
  budget. If reserves are declining, it may indicate an imbalance in the budget (e.g. if’ reserves are being
  used to hind on-going expenditures). Desired reserve levels are further discussed in Sections F and G
  of this document.

  Policy:
  The City shall endeavor to adopt a structurally balanced budget. Generally, this means that recurring
  expenditures should be covered by recurring revenues and that non-recurring revenues should be used

  159
 to fund non-recurring expenditures. The Finance Department shall incorporate information into its
budget presentation demonstrating the City’s progress in achieving a structurally balanced budget.

In order to achieve a structura]ly balanced budget, the City should consider the following:

  Employee compensation and non-recurring revenues  — With limited exceptions, non
  recurring revenues and reserves should not be used to fund employee compensation. One such
  exception might be a severe economic downturn where non-recurring revenues are
  temporarily used to ease the transition to an expenditure structure that is in line with new
  economic realities. Even this should only be done in the context of a plan to return to structural
  balance and replenish any reserves that had been ased.
  •  Operating and maintenance costs of capital assets purchased 4th non-recurring
  revenues While capital assets are often funded with non-recurring revenues, the City shall
  —

  he observant of the long-term operating and nuintenance costs of such purposes, to prevent
  the creation of new on-going expenditures that cannot be maintained by recurring revenues.
  •  Replacement of short-lived assets and non-recurring revenues The City shall prioritize
  —

  the use of non-recurring revenues to replace current assets that have outlived their useful hves
  over the purchase of entirely new assets, where the replacement of the expired or obsolete
  assets is critical to the maintenance of the City’s core programs. A replacement schedule for
  such assets is a good indicator of when to budget for these items.

  160
 P. REVENUES

  Purpose:
  The purpose of this policy is to establish guidelines for (a) the development of revenue estimates, (b)
  fee structures, and (c) use of new recurring and non-recurring revenues in order to achieve a
  structurally balanccd budget.

  Background:
  Revenue projections and assumptions are critical to budget decisions, particularly in order to achieve
  a structurally balanced budget. The Finance Department is responsible for coordinating all revenues
  esthmtes contained in the budget. Estimates are reached by analyzing historical revenue history.
  national and local economic trends and indices, and development patterns in the local economy. Many
  of the City’s key revenues are subject to siguificant fluctuation dependent on a nunther of economic
  fuctors. While it is difficult to always achieve accurate projections in a dynamic economic
  environment, it is important to have a consistent approach to projecting revenues in order for decision-
  makers to understand the basis used to project the resources available for the budget. Revenue should
  be proectcd in a way that is not likely to lead to a revenue shortfall. but also not to be so conservative
